zones.label: display
zones.summary: The LCD shows the number and the unit for whatever the meter is currently measuring.
facts: It reports the numeric result plus its unit — here 4.98 V on DC volts.
A small DC or AC marker tells you which kind of measurement is showing.
"OL" means overload: the reading is larger than the selected range can display. Turn the dial to a bigger range, or check you picked the right mode.

zones.label: dial
zones.summary: The rotary dial selects which of the meter's jobs is active.
facts: Each position picks one job: OFF, V for DC volts, mA for small currents, Ω for resistance, and the speaker-wave mark for continuity.
The dial must match the measurement you are attempting — a voltage reading taken in resistance mode is meaningless.
Leave it on OFF when you put the meter away, or the battery drains.

zones.label: COM
zones.summary: The black probe plugs in here, for every measurement mode without exception.
facts: COM is short for common — it is the meter's reference point, the equivalent of ground.
The black lead never moves. Whatever you are measuring, it stays in COM.
If a reading comes out negative, your two probes are simply the other way round; nothing is wrong.

zones.label: VΩmA
zones.summary: The red probe plugs in here for voltage, resistance and small-current measurements.
facts: This one jack serves volts, ohms and milliamps — the three modes you use most.
Larger currents use a separate high-current jack on most meters, often marked 10A. Moving the lead there and forgetting to move it back is a common way to blow the meter's fuse.
Red into VΩmA, black into COM, is the default setup for nearly everything in this book.

zones.label: black probe
facts: It runs from the COM jack to the point you are treating as the reference.
For voltage measurements this is usually the ground rail of your circuit.
Hold probes by the moulded grips, never by the metal tips.

zones.label: red probe
facts: It runs from the VΩmA jack to the point you want to measure.
For voltage you touch it to the node of interest while black stays at ground.
For current the circuit must be broken and both probes placed in the gap, so the current flows through the meter.

quiz.question: Which jack does the black probe plug into, no matter what you are measuring?
quiz.explanation: COM is the reference jack; the black lead never moves.

quiz.question: Which part decides whether the meter is measuring volts, ohms or current?
quiz.explanation: The rotary dial selects the mode, and it must match the measurement.

quiz.question: Where would you see the letters "OL", and what do they mean?
quiz.explanation: On the display — it means the value is beyond the selected range.

quiz.question: Which jack takes the red probe for voltage, resistance and milliamp readings?
quiz.explanation: The VΩmA jack serves all three of those modes.

quiz.question: Which lead do you move to the node you want to measure, leaving the other at ground?
quiz.explanation: The red probe is the measuring lead.
